Story & Plot

Sanjay Rajkot, known as Sikandar or Raja saab, is the generous and courageous king of Rajkot who finds himself clashing with a powerful minister. This conflict leads to a tragic accident and the death of his beloved wife, Saisri, who donates her organs to three individuals in Mumbai before passing away. In a ruthless attempt to break Sanjay's spirit, the minister targets these recipients, prompting the powerful protagonist to protect the less fortunate by standing up to corruption and greed.

Comedy & Entertainment

The film operates primarily as an action-packed revenge flick while featuring standard commercial elements meant to entertain the mass audience. While the central narrative is driven by tragedy, conflict, and a familiar setup, it attempts to engage viewers through its star power and stylistic presentation. The overall entertainment value relies heavily on the presence of the lead actors rather than dedicated comedic relief.

Performances & Direction

Salman Khan delivers a strong presence as the lead, anchoring the dramatic revenge premise. Rashmika Mandanna portrays his beloved wife Saisri, whose tragic passing sets the central plot in motion. The supporting cast features Sathyaraj as the powerful minister, alongside Sharman Joshi and Prateik Smita Patil.

Strengths

  • action sequences

Weaknesses

One of the major drawbacks of Sikandar is its sluggish pacing, weak plot, and tedious narrative. The predictable storyline is paired with a generic background score and clichéd storytelling that dilutes the emotional core. At over two and a half hours, the film feels overly stretched, and the outdated filmmaking style hinders engagement.

Final verdict

Sikandar offers action and style for audiences looking for a familiar revenge drama, but it is ultimately let down by a predictable plot and sluggish pacing. Viewers heavily invested in the lead cast may find moments of interest, but the stretched runtime and clichéd storytelling make it a challenging watch. It is recommended primarily for hardcore fans of the stars rather than those seeking a fresh cinematic experience.

Story & Plot

In a crumbling Indian town, three retired men stage a protest against machines taking over human jobs by pretending to be household appliances. Directed by Pranav Bhasin, this 10-minute short drama explores an unusual and thematic premise. The narrative centers on this silent, quirky resistance set against the backdrop of modernization and automation.

Comedy & Entertainment

The film brings a sense of dark humor and irony through its central premise of elderly men posing as appliances. While the overall tone leans toward drama, the absurdity of the protest generates quiet amusement and entertainment value. It relies heavily on the situational irony rather than explicit comedic gags.

Performances & Direction

The cast features Satish Kashyap, Devendra Dodke, Arindol Bagchi, Shubham Kujur, and Kalpana Gagdekar in a compact ensemble. The actors bring grounded presence to their roles as retired townsfolk making a silent statement against machines. Their commitment to portraying inanimate household objects anchors the short's unique vision.

Strengths

  • Unique and creative premise
  • Engaging short runtime
  • Solid ensemble performances
  • Thoughtful thematic background

Weaknesses

The extremely short 10-minute runtime leaves very little room to deeply explore the characters or the complexities of the automated threat. Additionally, the premise might stretch suspension of disbelief for some viewers who expect a more traditional narrative structure.

Final verdict

We Were Here is a brief, imaginative short that uses a strange form of protest to highlight modern anxieties about automation. Led by a capable cast including Satish Kashyap and Kalpana Gagdekar, it provides a quick and memorable watch. Recommended for viewers looking for concise and unconventional drama.
